name: Guam
summary_text: Guam stands under the United States framework as an unincorporated territory of the United States. Federal hate crime protection for gender identity has applied in Guam since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act.  Same-sex marriage has been lawful in Guam since June 2015. Chief Judge Frances M. Tydingco-Gatewood struck down the prohibition on 5 June 2015 in a case brought after Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero were denied a licence in April 2015, with the ruling effective at 8 a.m. on 9 June 2015. Licences were issued four days after the ruling, and the Guam Marriage Equality Act of 2015, passed on 11 August 2015, made marriage laws gender neutral. The ruling cited Latta v. Otter.  Airport screening in Guam follows Transportation Security Administration procedure, which applies in Guam as a United States territory. Body scanner and pat down procedures can disclose a transgender traveller's status to officers. Travellers may request alternative screening and may escalate problems on the spot. Guidance addresses pre flight packing and document and screening mismatches, and most transgender travellers pass screening without incident.  Guam is described as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment. That description is framed for LGBTQ people generally rather than for transgender people specifically.

name: Guyana
summary_text: Guyana criminalises consensual same-sex conduct under the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, retained in force after independence. Section 351 punishes gross indecency between men with up to two years imprisonment. Section 353 punishes buggery with life imprisonment, with related provisions covering attempted buggery. Some compilations cite the same offences as sections 352 to 354.  Prosecutions under these provisions are rare. The statutes nevertheless structure police encounters with lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons and sustain public stigma.  A constitutional savings clause bars judicial review of laws inherited at independence. The clause prevents courts from invalidating the inherited sexual offences even where they conflict with human rights guarantees.  Guyana provides no procedure for legal gender recognition. No provision for change of gender marker was identified in the sources.  The direct prohibition on cross-dressing, section 153(1)(xlvii) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act derived from an 1893 statute, was struck down on 13 November 2018. A regional court held in Quincy McEwan, Seon Clarke, Joseph Fraser, Seyon Persaud and SASOD v The Attorney General of Guyana that the provision was unconstitutionally vague, violated protection of the law and was contrary to freedom of expression and the rule of law. The case followed arrests of transgender women in 2009 with three nights detention, a challenge filed in 2010 with support from transgender and gay advocacy groups, a 2013 Chief Justice ruling that permitted cross-dressing unless for an improper purpose, affirmance by the Court of Appeal, and oral argument before the regional court beginning 28 June 2018.  Police abuse linked to the remaining laws is documented. The managing director of SASOD, Joel Simpson, reported in May 2019 that officers threatened men found in compromising positions with arrest under the sodomy laws to extract bribes, harassed same-sex couples in public spaces including seawalls and parks, and subjected complainants to secondary discrimination at stations. As a result complainants gave watered down accounts. Hate crimes often go unreported. After the 2018 ruling, residual loitering and vagrancy clauses remained usable against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons, principally sex workers.  Transgender women face documented street violence and failure of judicial protection. Petronella Trotman was stabbed in Georgetown in January 2017, sustaining a neck wound inflicted with scissors alongside an attack with glass bottles. On 2 March 2017 a magistrate, Dylon Bess, refused her entry to the Georgetown Magistrates Court unless she was dressed like a man. Her case against her attacker was then dismissed.  A hearing at the 191st session of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, requested by the Guyana Equality Forum on the impact of gender-based violence on migrant women, sex workers and transgender women, heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition. The Commission chair, Roberta Clarke, called on Guyana on 16 November 2024 to take urgent action. The record cited 69 documented cases of violence against trans women between 2018 and 2022.  Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist in Guyana. Constitutional protection on the ground of sexual orientation, approved unanimously in December 2000, was denied presidential assent before the March 2001 elections after religious opposition, and a reintroduction in 2003 was withdrawn without progress.  No hate-crime legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. On 16 June 2019 Simpson was beaten by six men after harassment at the Palm Court nightclub while waiting at Bourda Market. He filed a police complaint and called for hate-crime legislation. The Ministry of Social Protection condemned the attack while affirming acceptance. In July 2019 the Court of Appeal reduced a 57-year murder sentence imposed in 2015 on Clive Knights for the 2012 killing of Bert Whyte to 30 years for manslaughter after a claim of unwanted homosexual advances. Discrimination and violence by law enforcement, religious leaders and others are described as widespread, leading most lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons to conceal their orientation.  Official statements in favour of protection have not changed the statute book. In July 2019 Minister of Social Protection Amna Ally stated the government was working to remove legal gaps to prevent discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and affirmed the right to live free from violence, abuse and discrimination. In July 2025 five of six main parties, including the ruling party, supported decriminalisation. In September 2025 President Irfaan Ali promised to decriminalise in cooperation with SASOD. The criminal provisions remained in force.
